By him, the chief of Sankhyas, who saw the truth well, I was taught threefold liberation, and I did not stray from the kingdom.
mahabharata:12:308.28	I, with that whole threefold livelihood joined with liberation, roam alone, free of attachment, standing in the supreme state.
mahabharata:12:308.29	Detachment is the supreme rule of this liberation; and detachment arises from knowledge alone, by which one is freed.
mahabharata:12:308.30	By knowledge one makes effort; by effort the great is gained; that success which goes beyond the span of life is for release from the great pairs.
mahabharata:12:308.31	This supreme understanding of freedom from the pairs I have gained right here, with delusion gone, moving about with attachments released.
mahabharata:12:308.32	As a field softened and flooded with water brings forth a sprout, so the action of men brings forth rebirth.
mahabharata:12:308.33	And as seed that has been roasted in a pot, wherever it is, does not sprout, since it is seedless, though reaching the condition of a cause of sprouting,
mahabharata:12:308.34	so by the blessed mendicant Shikha's teaching, knowledge made seedless in me does not sprout in objects.
mahabharata:12:308.35	I am not attached to anything, nor to any harm or possession; I am not drawn to these, since attachment and fault are useless.
mahabharata:12:308.36	One who would anoint my right arm with sandal and one who would cut my left with an adze are both equal to me.
mahabharata:12:308.37	Happy am I, my aim attained, clod, stone and gold alike; freed from attachment, I stand in the kingdom, distinguished from other wearers of the triple staff.
mahabharata:12:308.38	In liberation threefold steadfastness has been seen by earlier great sages: knowledge above the world, and renunciation of all actions.
mahabharata:12:308.39	Some who know the shastra of liberation speak of steadfastness in knowledge; others, the ascetics who see the subtle, of steadfastness in action.
mahabharata:12:308.40	Leaving both, knowledge and action, alone: this third steadfastness was declared by that great soul.
mahabharata:12:308.41	In restraint, in rule, in aversion, in desire, in possessions, in pride, in hypocrisy and in affection, they are the same as householders.
mahabharata:12:308.42	If there is liberation by some knowledge in the triple staff and the like, why not in the parasol and the like, when the cause of possession is the same?
mahabharata:12:308.43	For whatever reason someone has a purpose, he relies on that thing; everyone has his own possessions.
mahabharata:12:308.44	One who, seeing fault in the household life, goes to another stage, giving up and taking, is not freed from attachment either.
mahabharata:12:308.45	In rulership, equal, of the nature of restraint and favour, by what mark are royal sages, mendicants and teachers freed?
mahabharata:12:308.46	Or if, in true lordship, one is freed by knowledge alone, why are they not freed, standing in the supreme state?
mahabharata:12:308.47	Wearing ochre, shaven head, the triple staff, the water-pot: these marks are excessive; they are not for liberation: so I hold.
mahabharata:12:308.48	If, with this mark present, knowledge alone is the cause here for release from sorrow, then the mark alone is useless.
mahabharata:12:308.49	Or, if one's mind is set on the mark seeing the loosening of sorrow, why is that same common purpose not seen in the parasol and the rest?
mahabharata:12:308.50	In having nothing there is liberation; in having something there is no bondage; a creature is freed by knowledge, whether having something or not.
mahabharata:12:308.51	Therefore in dharma, wealth and desire, and in the possession of a kingdom, these seats of bondage, know me standing in the unbound state.
mahabharata:12:308.52	The snare made of royal lordship, whose bond is the seat of affection, has been cut by me here with the sharp sword of renunciation on the stone of liberation.
mahabharata:12:308.53	Such, I am freed, mendicant, having found faith in you; your colour is not real; I shall tell; hear it.
mahabharata:12:308.54	Your delicacy, such form, excellent body and age: all these are yours, and your rule is in doubt.
mahabharata:12:308.55	And your conduct, not befitting this mark: 'Is he freed or not?' By this my possession has been violated.
mahabharata:12:308.56	For one who is freed and joined with desire there is no triple staff; this is not guarded by you; the freed one has no guarding.
mahabharata:12:308.57	And from resorting to my side, hear what your transgression is, who by nature resort to my earlier possession:
mahabharata:12:308.58	By whom was entry made by you into my kingdom and city, or by whose permission did you enter my heart?
mahabharata:12:308.59	You are the chief of the best class, a brahmana; I am a kshatriya; there is no union of the two; do not make a mixing of classes.
mahabharata:12:308.60	You live in the dharmas of liberation, while I am in the householder's stage; and this is a second mixing of stages, quite clear.
mahabharata:12:308.61	Of the same lineage or different, you do not know me, I do not know you; for you entering one of the same lineage is a third mixing of lineage.
mahabharata:12:308.62	Or if your husband is alive, or away somewhere, a wife of another is unapproachable: the fourth mixing of dharma.
mahabharata:12:308.63	You, such, resolve these unfit acts, intent on some purpose, whether joined with ignorance or false knowledge.
mahabharata:12:308.64	Or if you are independent, then by some fault of yours; if you have heard anything, all is done in vain.
mahabharata:12:308.65	This is another, third thing in you, destroyer of the touch of feeling: the mark of a spoiled one is seen; it has been declared and revealed.
mahabharata:12:308.66	Your purpose is not in me alone; wishing victory in victory, you wish to conquer this whole assembly of mine too.
mahabharata:12:308.67	Thus indeed you again press your own view, to defeat my side and to set up your own side.
mahabharata:12:308.68	You, bewildered by impatience of your own and the delusion of prosperity, again create the weapon of yoga, like poison and nectar in one.
mahabharata:12:308.69	For two who wish it, the union of woman and man is like nectar; and non-union for the unattached, there the fault is like poison.
mahabharata:12:308.70	Do not question, know it well, keep to your own shastra; this inquiry 'is he freed or not' was made by you for me; all this you ought not to hide from me.
mahabharata:12:308.71	If you, for your own business, or for another king, are hiding your truth in a disguise, you ought not to hide it from me.
mahabharata:12:308.72	One should not go falsely to a king, nor in any way to a twice-born, nor to a woman endowed with womanly virtues; those who go falsely are killed.
mahabharata:12:308.73	For kings, lordship is their strength; for knowers of Brahman, Brahman; for women, beauty, youth and good fortune are the highest strength.
mahabharata:12:308.74	Therefore, one wishing his own end should approach the strong with these strengths honestly; for dishonesty leads to destruction.
mahabharata:12:308.75	You ought to tell truly your birth, learning, conduct, feeling, your nature, and the business of your coming.
Thus addressed by the king with these disagreeable, unfitting and incoherent words, Sulabha did not tremble.
When the king had spoken, Sulabha of lovely appearance began to speak words yet more lovely.
Free of nine faults that spoil speech and intellect, and endowed with ten virtues, with fitting meaning:
subtlety, number, sequence, determination and purpose: these five kinds of meaning, king, are called speech.
Hear the good marks of each of these, subtlety and the rest, as they are being unfolded by words and by phrase.
When knowledge operates in differing knowables by difference, then the surpassing understanding is called subtlety.
The measure of faults and virtues by division, in view of some purpose, is to be taken as number.
'This first, this afterward': what is to be said is intended; the knowers of speech call that order.
Having pledged specially regarding dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, at the end of the speech 'this is that' is said; that is determination.
Where the highest degree of sorrows born of wish and aversion arises, the livelihood there, king, is held to be the purpose.
Subtlety and the rest, as told, lord of the people, are joined in one meaning; hear my speech.
I shall speak to you the highest: joined with meaning, undivided in meaning, not turned aside, not excessive, not rough, not doubtful.
Not joined with heavy syllables, not facing away, not untrue, not opposed to the three aims, not uncollected,
not deficient, not with a word misused, not said out of order, not with remainder, not by alternative, not causeless or reasonless.
I shall not speak from desire, anger, fear, greed, dejection, ignobleness, shame, pity or pride in any way.
When speaker, hearer and speech are perfect, king, meeting in the wish to speak, then the matter is revealed.
But when the speaker, in what is to be said, despises the hearer and speaks for his own purpose or another's, speech does not take root.
And if a man, giving up his own purpose, speaks for another's purpose, suspicion arises in him; that speech too is faulty.
But the speaker who speaks a meaning not opposed to both the hearer and himself is the speaker, king, not another.
This speech, full of meaning and joined with the wealth of speech: hear it, king, with mind undistracted and one-pointed.
Who are you, whose, whence? I was asked by you; to that, king, hear this answer with one mind.
As lac and wood and dust stick well together with drops of water, so, king, is the origin of creatures here.
Sound, touch, taste, form, smell and the five senses, and the self separate, are ten selves, joined like lac and wood.
There is no urging among them: so it is settled; knowledge in each is not in the self, nor in the others.
The eye does not know the eye, you; the ear does not abide in the self; so they do not act upon one another by deviation; joined, they are not born, like dust here with water.
They depend on outer virtues; hear those too: form, eye and light are three causes in seeing; as here, so in other knowings and knowables.
In that interval between knowledge and knowable, another quality named mind, by which one deliberates good and bad in decision.
A twelfth quality there is intellect, by which one decides, with doubt first, in things to be known.
Then in the twelve there is another quality named sattva, by which a creature is inferred to be of great or little goodness.
Another is the fourteenth quality there, the knower of the field, by which this one thinks "this is mine" and does not think it.
Then a fifteenth quality there, king: the totality of the aggregate of the several parts, so it is said here.
Another quality there is the sixteenth, the aggregate, in which these two qualities, shape and manifestation, rest.
Pleasure and pain, old age and death, gain and loss, dear and undear: this is the nineteenth, held to be the conjunction of pairs.
Beyond the nineteen, another quality named time; by these twenty know the origin and dissolution of beings.
And this aggregate is wonderful; the five great elements, and being and non-being, the two other qualities that illuminate.
So the twenty qualities and the seven that are remembered: the rule, semen and strength are three other qualities.
The twenty-first and the ten are held to be parts by count; where all are present together, that is called the body.
Of these parts some want the unmanifest, nature; another, seeing grossly, sees the manifest.
Whether unmanifest or manifest, twofold or fourfold, those who think on the self see the nature of all beings.
This unmanifest nature has become manifest through the parts: I, you, king of kings, and the other embodied beings.
States beginning with the placing of a drop, arisen from semen and blood, by whose falling alone the embryo is formed.
From the embryo the swelling arises, from the swelling the flesh-mass, from the flesh-mass the formation of the limbs, and nails and hair from the limbs.
In the ninth month complete, Maithila, of the born creature, name and form arise, woman or man by the mark.
Seeing a form newly born, with copper-red nails and fingers, then it becomes the form of a child, and the earlier is not found in the form.
From childhood to youth and from youth to old age; by this sequence the earlier is not found.
The separation of the parts, of different purposes, goes on moment by moment in all beings, but from subtlety it is not perceived.
Neither their dissolution nor their origin is seen, king; the course of state to state is like the flame of a lamp.
And with its origin so, running like a good horse constantly, who is this of the whole world, whence, or whence not?
Whose is this, or whose not? Whence is this, or not? What relation is there among beings even with their own members here?
As fire arises from the sun, from the jewel and from the plants, so beings arise from the combination of parts.
As you see the self in the self by the self, so why do you not see the self in another by the self? If you resolve upon equality of self and other...
then why do you ask me 'who are you, whose?' For one freed from the pairs, 'this is mine, this is not,' what purpose is there in asking 'who are you, whose, whence?'
He who has made enemy, friend and neutral, victory, peace and war, lord of the earth, what mark of the freed is in him?
He who does not know the sevenfold manifest in the three aims in actions, and who is attached to the three aims, what mark of the freed is in him?
He who has no equal eye in the dear and undear, the weak and strong, what mark of the freed is in him?
The conceit you have in your liberation, while unfreed, king, should be turned aside by friends, as a deranged man by physicians.
Looking at those and those places of attachment, scourge of foes, he should see in the self by the self; what mark of the freed is in him?
Hear from me these other subtle seats of attachment, resorting to liberation, that go on in four limbs.
The king who rules this whole earth under one parasol dwells in just one city.
In that city he occupies just one house; in the house, one bed in which he lies at night.
Half the bed, too, a woman occupies first; so by this connection he is joined with its fruit.
So too in enjoyments, in food and clothing, in measured virtues, regarding restraint and favour:
a king is ever dependent, and engaged in small things; in peace and war where is the king's independence?
In pleasures of women and recreation, he is always unfree; in counsel and in the assembly of ministers how is he independent?
When he commands others, then his independence is said; but he is made helplessly to do things in this and that quality.
Wanting to sleep, he cannot sleep because of people seeking business; even permitted to sleep in bed, he is woken helplessly.
Bathe, anoint, drink, eat, offer to the fires, sacrifice, speak, listen: thus he is made helplessly to act by others.
Men approach and approach him begging always, and, guarding his wealth, he cannot bring himself to give to a great multitude.
In giving, his treasury is lost; if he refuses, enmity; in a moment faults that cause detachment arise in him.
He fears the wise, the brave and the rich even in one place; in safety there is fear for a king from those who always attend him.
When these whom I have named turn bad, king, from them fear arises in him, see what kind.
Each king in his own house, each householder in his own house, doing restraint and favour, is equal to King Janaka.
Sons, wives, the self, treasury, friends and hoard are shared with others; by those and those causes they are his.
If a country is destroyed, a city burnt, the chief elephant dead, he is tormented by false knowledge in these common things of the world.
Unfreed from mental sorrows born of wish, aversion and love, by diseases like headache, and by the falling kind,
struck by those and those pairs, suspicious on every side, he serves a kingdom with many foes, counting the nights.
That is very little happiness, much sorrow, without essence; who would take a kingdom, and having taken it, find peace?
This city and kingdom, army, treasury and ministers which you think 'mine': whose are they, or not, king?
Ally, minister, city, realm, rod, treasury and the king: this sevenfold wheel-aggregate is called a kingdom, king.
In this sevenfold kingdom, standing like a triple staff, joined to each other's qualities, which is greater than which by quality?
At those and those times that member is the more distinguished; by which a work is accomplished, it becomes chief.
The sevenfold aggregate and three others, best of kings, together are the tenfold group, and enjoy the kingdom as a king.
The king who is of great energy and devoted to kshatriya dharma should be content with a tenth part, and the others with a tenth less.
There is no king not shared; there is no kingdom without a king; where there is no kingdom, how dharma? Where there is no dharma, how the supreme?
The supreme dharma here, the purifier of king and kingdom, is that of which the earth is the fee: there is no horse sacrifice like it.
I, Maithila, can tell these actions and sorrows of kingship by hundreds or even thousands.
I have no attachment even to my own body; how to another's possession? You ought not to speak so to one such as me, freed.
Surely you heard whole liberation from Panchashikha, with its means, with the Upanishad, with its appendages and its settlement?
How then, king, is there attachment again in parasols and the like, for you freed from attachment, standing over the snares?
I think what you heard was not heard; or what you heard was falsely heard; or it was heard like heard, and what you heard was another heard.
And yet you stand in these worldly designations; bound by attachment and obstruction, you are, to me, common.
The entry I made into you by goodness: what harm was done to you by it, if you are wholly freed?
This is the rule in the dharmas of ascetics: dwelling in empty places; in occupying an empty place what is spoiled, and of whom?
Not with hands, not with arms, not with feet and thighs, sinless one, not with any other limbs do I touch you, lord of men.
By one born in a great family, modest, far-sighted, this should not be said in an assembly: what is done between two, whether good or bad.
These brahmanas are teachers and these ministers are the best teachers; you too are a teacher of them; so is mutual respect.
So, having considered this and testing what is to be said and not said, this union of woman and man should not be spoken by you in the assembly.
As water standing on a lotus leaf stays on the leaf without touching it, so I shall dwell in you, Maithila.
And if, though I do not touch, you know some touch of mine, how did that mendicant make your knowledge seedless?
You, fallen from the household life and not having gained liberation hard to know, live in the middle of both, a wind-bag of liberation.
For one freed, knowing, with the freed, in oneness and separateness, in the meeting of being and non-being, there arises no mixing of classes.
In the separateness of classes and stages, for one who has seen the purpose and does not see separateness, knowing 'not one thing and another,' nothing goes on as one thing and another.
As a jasmine in the hand, milk in the jasmine, flies in the milk, we are separate supports by union of support and supported.
There is no being of milk in the jasmine, nor of flies in the milk; these states themselves resort, not to another's support.
By the separateness of stages and the difference of classes and mutual separateness, how is there mixing of classes for you?
I am not of the highest class by birth, nor a vaishya, nor lower; I am of your own class, king, of pure womb, unfallen.
There was a royal sage named Pradhana; it has come plainly to your ear; know me, born in his family, as Sulabha by name.
Drona, Shatashringa and Vakradvara the mountain, in my ancestors' sacrifices, were piled with Maghavan.
Born in that family, I have no husband like me; trained in the dharmas of liberation, I roam alone, keeping the sage's vow.
I am not disguised in a guise, not proud of another's wealth, not a maker of mixing of dharma; I keep my vow in my own dharma.
I am not unsteady in my own promise, not speaking without consideration; I have not come to you without consideration, lord of the people.
Hearing of your mind turning to liberation, I, wishing good, came here to inquire about this liberation of yours.
I do not say this as belonging to a party, neither of my side nor of another's; one freed is not freed, and one calm is not calm.
As a mendicant would stay a night in an empty city house, so I shall stay this night in this body of yours.
Honoured by the gift of a seat and the hospitality of speech, I shall sleep well and, pleased, go tomorrow, Maithila."
Hearing these words, reasoned and meaningful, the king found nothing more to say after that.
[Bhishma said:] A father instructed his son, who was roaming without fear in common good conduct, having taught him the whole of study:

Practise dharma, son; cold and heat are very sharp; always conquer hunger, thirst and wind, master of your senses.
mahabharata:12:309.4	Truth, honesty, freedom from anger, freedom from envy, self-control, austerity, non-violence and non-cruelty, protect by rule.
mahabharata:12:309.5	Stand in truth, delight in dharma, giving up all dishonesty; sustain the course of life with what remains after gods and guests.
mahabharata:12:309.6	In a body like a bowl of foam, with life perched like a bird, impermanent, dear companion, how do you sleep, my son?
mahabharata:12:309.7	While enemies are watchful, awake, ever joined, seeking an opening, you, a child, do not awaken.
mahabharata:12:309.8	As years are counted and life wastes away and living remains little, why do you not rise and run?
mahabharata:12:309.9	Those who strive for this world, increasing flesh and blood, fall asleep over the tasks for the next world, utter unbelievers.
mahabharata:12:309.12	Considering the view of those aged who see dharma, restrain by supreme intellect the mind that strays from the path.
mahabharata:12:309.13	With a mind of the day, saying 'tomorrow is far,' fearless all-eaters, senseless, do not see the land of action.
mahabharata:12:309.14	Resorting to the ladder of dharma, climb a little by little; you wrap yourself like a silkworm and do not awaken.
mahabharata:12:309.15	The unbelieving, who break the limits, unsteady like a collapsing bank, leave on the left, trusting, like a reed-man swollen.
mahabharata:12:309.16	Desire, anger and death, the river with the five senses as waters: making a boat of steadiness, cross the hard places of birth.
mahabharata:12:309.17	When the world is struck by death, when it is oppressed by old age, when unfailing ones fall, cross by the vehicle of dharma.
mahabharata:12:309.18	When death seeks you standing or lying, how do you find ease? Why are you suddenly destroyed by death?
mahabharata:12:309.19	Death takes the man gathering, unsated in desires, as a she-wolf takes a lamb.
mahabharata:12:309.20	With the flame gathered in order, great, made of the intellect of dharma, a lamp must be carried with effort when entering darkness.
mahabharata:12:309.21	Falling into nets of bodies, sometimes in the human state a creature gains brahminhood; protect that, son.
mahabharata:12:309.22	For the body of a brahmana is not born for desire and wealth; here it is for affliction and austerity, and hereafter incomparable happiness.
mahabharata:12:309.23	Brahminhood is gained by many austerities; having gained it one should not waste it for a trifle; ever joined in study, austerity and self-control, striving for safety, ever strive skilfully.
mahabharata:12:309.24	This unmanifest-natured, part-bodied one, subtle in self, with moments for ligaments, winks for hairs, seasons for mouth, with white and black eyes of equal strength, with measure for limbs, runs: the horse of men's life.
mahabharata:12:309.25	Seeing that which goes on ceaselessly, of fierce speed, ever moving here without waiting, if your eye is not led by others, hearing the supreme, let your mind be set on dharma.
mahabharata:12:309.26	Those who have strayed from the conduct of dharma and desire, shouting always, joined with the unwished, are afflicted with bodies pierced by pain, by many strong impressions of adharma.
mahabharata:12:309.27	The king ever devoted to dharma, protector of the good, looking at the virtuous, grants them worlds; and also gives various goals to those who act otherwise, happiness not before gained and blameless.
mahabharata:12:309.28	Dogs, fearsome crows and groups of vultures and birds, drinking blood, devour the man who has strayed from the teacher's word in the slaughter of men.
mahabharata:12:309.29	The limits fixed by the Self-born, which the tenfold qualities break through by following the mind, he enters very painful dwelling in the forest of the ancestors, that sinner.
mahabharata:12:309.30	The man who is greedy, fond of untruth, ever delighting in deceit and cheating, is a maker of unhappiness by deposits; he goes to the lowest hell and feels great pain, a doer of evil deeds.
mahabharata:12:309.31	You plunge into the hot Vaitarani, the great river, your limbs cut by leaf-forests, lying fallen in the axe-forest, dwelling in great hell, in great pain.
mahabharata:12:309.32	You boast of great feats and do not look to the beyond; you do not awaken to the death-bringing that long has been coming.
mahabharata:12:309.33	Why sit when the great, dreadful, destroying fear has risen for you who are to depart? Make arrangement for happiness.
mahabharata:12:309.34	Before you die you are led to Yama's presence by death's command; make effort in honesty against those dreadful ones.
mahabharata:12:309.35	Before the lord who does not know sorrow takes away the life here with root and kinsmen, there is none to restrain Yama.
mahabharata:12:309.36	Before the wind blows that goes before Yama, you are led alone; do what concerns the other world.
mahabharata:12:309.37	Before the ender's wind blows on you with hiccup, before the directions swirl for you at the coming of great fear,
mahabharata:12:309.38	before memory is blocked, son, make the best concentration for yourself who are going in distraction.
Then, having adorned that maiden in clean garments, King Duryodhana gave her to Agni the great-souled.
How, lord of the hosts of gods, having served as your priest, could I sacrifice for the mortal Marutta, Pakashasana?
I too shall fast, as this one is my teacher, if this king does not eat, and the glorious Gandhari.
Thousand-headed, with a body like a mountain, red-faced, he left his own body there, and the sea received him rightly, and the divine and holy rivers of the nagas.
This is the third test, king, made by me; you cannot be moved by reasons from your nature, Partha.
